bug_description.original: The SAS7BDAT reader contains insufficient bounds checking, which allows a buffer overrun when reading the subheader pointers.
bug_description.normalized: The staged 8192-byte witness drives `sas_read_header` to select 64-bit SAS layout (`a2 == 0x33`) with `page_size == 1024`, so later page parsing treats each page as a 40-byte header followed by 24-byte subheader-pointer slots. The same header also seeds `ctx->header_size` and `ctx->page_count`, which control the meta-pass, the AMD reverse scan, and the later all-pages pass2 loop. Static inspection of the staged bytes proves meta pass1 reads pages at offsets 1024, 2048, and 3072 as non-DATA/non-compressed with subheader counts 3, 0, and 0, then stops when the page at offset 4096 is DATA; those visible pages satisfy pass1's `ctx->page_header_size + subheader_count*lshp <= ctx->page_size` guard. The saved AddressSanitizer stack then proves the parser rewinds and enters `sas7bdat_parse_all_pages_pass2`, where a later non-DATA, non-compressed pass2 page reaches `sas7bdat_parse_page_pass2`. In pass2, `subheader_count` controls the `for (i=0; i<subheader_count; i++)` walk from `shp = &page[ctx->page_header_size]`, but unlike pass1 there is no pre-loop table-fit check and no per-slot remaining-bytes check before `sas_read8(&shp[0], ...)`. The crash shows that on one pass2 body entry `shp` had already advanced to `page + 1024`, so `sas_read8` performed an 8-byte read from the first byte past the 1024-byte heap page. The saved artifacts do not uniquely identify which pass2 page index in the staged blob supplied that exhausting loop bound, so this GT grounds the bug at the witnessed pass2 cursor state and the missing source-level check that the patch adds through `sas7bdat_parse_subheader_pointer()`.

source.description: First project-code statement that consumes attacker-controlled SAS header bytes and selects the 64-bit layout used on the crashing path.
source.value_from: The exact staged 8192-byte `poc` has header byte 0x20 == 0x33 (`SAS_ALIGNMENT_OFFSET_4`), and the same header later supplies `page_size = 0x400` at bytes 0xc8..0xcb. Those attacker-controlled header fields pick the 64-bit pointer format used by the crashing pass2 read.

sink.description: AddressSanitizer crash site. `data` aliases `&shp[0]` on the crashing pass2 body entry after the subheader-pointer cursor has reached the end of the 1024-byte heap page.
sink.note: The saved sanitizer trace reports `heap-buffer-overflow` READ of size 8 at this line on address `0x619000000480`, exactly 0 bytes to the right of the 1024-byte region allocated in `readstat_parse_sas7bdat`.

root_cause.description: Pass2 uses the attacker-controlled `subheader_count` to walk subheader-pointer records from `shp = &page[ctx->page_header_size]` without first proving that the pointer table fits inside the page or that the current slot still contains the 64-bit pointer fields about to be read.
root_cause.note: Pass1 rejects `ctx->page_header_size + subheader_count*lshp > ctx->page_size` at line 665 before entering its analogous walk, but pass2 performs no equivalent table-fit check and reads `offset` and `len` before validating the slot. The fix adds `sas7bdat_parse_subheader_pointer()` so the remaining bytes are checked before any `sas_read8` or `sas_read4` field access.

tainted_value_origin.description: Pass2 materializes the current page header's attacker-controlled subheader-count field into `subheader_count`; that scalar becomes the only loop bound controlling how many 24-byte pointer slots are walked from `shp = page + 40`.

parser_admitted.description: This pass2 call is reached only after `sas_read_header`, the meta-pass scan, the AMD reverse scan, and the rewind to `ctx->header_size`. The saved ASan stack confirms the crash happens inside this pass2 invocation.

coarse_trace.summary: The harness exposes the exact 8192-byte witness through `rt_buffer_t` / `rt_buffer_ctx_t` and calls `readstat_parse_sas7bdat` on that in-memory file.

Header parsing materializes 64-bit page layout, `page_size == 1024`, and a header-derived `page_count`; `readstat_parse_sas7bdat` copies those values into `ctx` and allocates a 1024-byte heap page buffer.

Using header-derived page offsets, meta pass1 examines the exact staged pages at offsets 1024, 2048, and 3072, then stops at the DATA page at offset 4096; after the AMD reverse scan returns, `readstat_parse_sas7bdat` rewinds to `ctx->header_size` and enters pass2.

On the crashing pass2 iteration, a non-DATA, non-compressed page supplies the `subheader_count` that keeps the `shp` walk running without pass1's table-fit guard or any per-slot remaining-bytes check.

By the crashing body entry, the pass2 cursor has reached `page + 1024`, and `sas_read8` reads 8 bytes from the first byte past the 1024-byte page allocation, matching the saved AddressSanitizer trace.

fine_trace.note: Wraps the exact 8192-byte witness as the in-memory file read later through ReadStat's `readstat_io_t` callbacks.

Header byte 0x20 equals `0x33` (`SAS_ALIGNMENT_OFFSET_4`), so `sas_read_header` selects 64-bit SAS layout. Later page parsing therefore uses 24-byte subheader-pointer slots and the 64-bit `sas_read8` field loads.

fine_trace.code:
hinfo->header_size = bswap ? byteswap4(header_size) : header_size;
hinfo->page_size = bswap ? byteswap4(page_size) : page_size;
fine_trace.note: Header bytes 0xc4..0xc7 decode little-endian to `header_size == 1024`, and bytes 0xc8..0xcb decode to `page_size == 1024`. Those two header-derived sizes later determine where every page starts on disk and how large the reused heap page buffer is.

Because step 2 selected 64-bit layout, the parser fixes `page_header_size = 40` and `subheader_pointer_size = 24`. Those constants define the page-type field offset (`page+32`), the subheader-count field offset (`page+36`), and the later `shp += 24` cursor stride.

Header bytes 0xcc..0xd3 materialize `hinfo->page_count`, the scalar later used as the loop bound for meta pass1, the AMD reverse scan, and all-pages pass2. With `header_size == page_size == 1024`, the staged blob physically contains seven full page-sized blocks after the header, but the saved artifacts do not uniquely map this raw page-count field to the specific pass2 page that later crashes.
The header-derived sizes, page-count scalar, and pointer stride are copied into `ctx`. Those fields drive every later page-offset calculation and both pass1 and pass2 page loops.
Allocates `ctx->page`, the 1024-byte heap buffer reused for every later page read. AddressSanitizer identifies the crashing read as starting exactly at the first byte after this allocation.

Using `ctx->header_size + i*ctx->page_size`, meta pass1 reads exact page headers at on-disk offsets 1024, 2048, and 3072. Their page-type words are `0x2020` (non-DATA/non-compressed) and their subheader counts are `3`, `0`, and `0`, so pass1's `40 + subheader_count*24 <= 1024` guard accepts them. The next page header at offset 4096 has bytes `20 01`, whose masked value classifies it as DATA, so meta pass1 stops there and records `last_examined_page_pass1 = 3`.

This pass2 call is reached only after the preceding AMD reverse scan `sas7bdat_parse_amd_pages_pass1(last_examined_page_pass1, ctx)` returns successfully and the seek at line 1071 rewinds to `ctx->header_size`. The saved ASan stack proves that this all-pages pass2 invocation began, but the saved artifacts do not uniquely identify which later pass2 page instance is the crashing one.

Pass2 copies one full 1024-byte page from the attacker-controlled file into the heap page buffer for the current loop index. The later crash occurs while interpreting this current buffer as a page header plus subheader-pointer table, but the saved artifacts do not uniquely identify which pass2 page index it is.

Line 744 can execute only in the `else if (!(page_type & SAS_PAGE_TYPE_COMP))` arm, so the crashing pass2 iteration necessarily used a page whose header was not DATA and not compressed, even though the saved artifacts do not tie that header to a unique page index.

Pass2 materializes the active page header's attacker-controlled `subheader_count`. That scalar is the only loop bound for how many 24-byte pointer slots will be walked from `shp = page + 40` on this page.
Initializes the subheader-pointer cursor to the first slot immediately after the 40-byte page header, i.e. `shp = page + 40` on the crashing pass2 page.

Root cause. Pass2 enters the pointer walk using step 11's attacker-controlled count and step 12's cursor base, but unlike pass1 it never checks `ctx->page_header_size + subheader_count*lshp > ctx->page_size` before the loop and never checks that the current slot still contains the 64-bit pointer fields before reading them. The fix adds `sas7bdat_parse_subheader_pointer()` precisely to enforce that per-slot remaining-bytes check before any field load.

Across earlier completed loop trips, this statement advances `shp` by `lshp == 24` each time. The saved ASan report says the crashing read starts 0 bytes to the right of the 1024-byte page allocation, so on the crashing body entry the cursor had already advanced from `page + 40` to `page + 1024`; the saved artifacts do not resolve which exact page supplied those earlier trips.

Because step 2 selected 64-bit mode, pass2's first pointer-field load is `sas_read8(&shp[0], ...)`. On the crashing body entry, `&shp[0]` aliases `page + page_size`, so this read starts at the first byte past the heap page before any offset or length check can run.

ASan sink. `data` is `&shp[0]` from step 15, so this memcpy performs an 8-byte read starting at the first byte past the 1024-byte `ctx->page` allocation. The saved stack is `sas_read8 -> sas7bdat_parse_page_pass2 -> sas7bdat_parse_all_pages_pass2 -> readstat_parse_sas7bdat`.

sanitizer_ground_truth.evidence_note: One staged vulnerable reproduction and the independently saved default crash trace show the same AddressSanitizer heap-buffer-overflow read in `sas_read8`. The saved artifacts fix the sink, the missing pass2 check, and the 1024-byte allocation context, but they do not uniquely identify which pass2 page index in the staged blob supplied the exhausting loop bound.

cross_validation.root_cause_matches_allocation_context: The allocation context creates the 1024-byte `ctx->page` buffer, and the missing pass2 table-fit / remaining-slot check is what later lets `shp` reach `page + page_size` before `sas_read8` reads from it.

poc.trigger: Stage 01's saved vulnerable run on `gt_results/arvo_12662/poc` reproduced `AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 8 in sas_read8`, matching the staged sanitizer trace.

format.name: Exact staged 8192-byte SAS7BDAT witness
format.contract: Verified trigger semantics are limited to the exact staged 8192-byte blob `poc` with SHA-256 `351fca8b7fbe4d54d430420b8b32d9b7e75fa9e7ac70cf069bffe9d7ec91888a`. Its header bytes select 64-bit SAS layout (`a2 == 0x33`) and `page_size == 0x400`; static inspection also proves meta pass1 classifies the first three on-disk pages after the header as non-DATA/non-compressed and the fourth as DATA. The saved Stage 01 run proves that this exact blob still reaches `sas7bdat_parse_all_pages_pass2` and then crashes in `sas_read8` from `sas7bdat_parse_page_pass2` when the pass2 subheader-pointer cursor reaches the end of a 1024-byte page. The saved artifacts do not uniquely resolve which pass2 page index or exact on-disk page-header field in the current staged blob supplied that exhausting loop bound, so this contract does not generalize to a numeric `subheader_count` range, a specific `page_count` interpretation, or any broader SAS7BDAT input class.
